title: Multi-Account Cheating

description.intro: Our company runs an online game where the terms of service state that each person can only have one account. We have a list of usernames and the (unordered) list of IP addresses that they have ever connected from. We say two users are suspected of belonging to the same person if the list of IPs is the same. Return whether any two lists contain the exact same set of IPs.
examples:
Example 2: users = [
  ("alice", ["1.1.1.1"]),
  ("bob", ["2.2.2.2"])
]
Output: False. No two users have the same IPs.

Example 3: users = []
Output: False. There are no users.
description.approach:
The length of users is at most 10^5
Each username is non-empty and unique
Each list of IPs has between 1 and 10 IPs
All IPs are unique and follow the IPv4 format
Each octet is a number between 0 and 255

Conceptually, we want to look for duplicates in the lists of IPs. However, arrays are mutable, so we can't use them directly as set elements in most languages. We need to transform them into an immutable type first.

The lists could contain the same IPs but in a different order, so we sort them before transforming them into an immutable type (like a tuple in Python or a string in JavaScript). The sorted version of each list is like a canonical representation shared by all the lists with the same elements.

For each user:

Sort their list of IPs to get a canonical representation
Convert the sorted list to an immutable type
Check if we've seen this canonical representation before
If we have, return True since we found a duplicate
Otherwise, add it to our set of seen lists
If we get through all users without finding a duplicate, return False.

complexity:
Time & Space Analysis
n: the number of users

k: the maximum number of IPs per user (at most 10)

Time: O(n) - for each user, we sort their list of IPs which would take O(k log k) time. We then check if the sorted list exists in our set, which takes O(k) time for the comparison. This is done n times. Since k is bounded to 10 this simplifies to just O(n).

Extra space: O(n) - in the worst case, we may need to store all unique IP lists in our set. Each list has at most k IPs, but since k is bounded to 10 the n*k analysis simplifies to O(n).

tests.python:
def run_tests():
  tests = [
      # Example 
      ([("mike", ["203.0.3.10", "208.51.0.5", "52.0.2.5"]),
        ("bob", ["111.0.0.10", "222.0.0.5", "222.0.0.8"]),
          ("bob2", ["222.0.0.5", "222.0.0.8", "111.0.0.10"])], True),
      # Additional test cases
      ([], False),
      ([("alice", ["1.1.1.1"])], False),
      ([("alice", ["1.1.1.1", "2.2.2.2"]),
        ("bob", ["2.2.2.2", "1.1.1.1"])], True),
      ([("alice", ["1.1.1.1"]), ("bob", ["2.2.2.2"])], False),
  ]
  for users, want in tests:
    got = multi_account_cheating(users)
    assert got == want, f"\nmulti_account_cheating({users}): got: {        got}, want: {want}\n"

run_tests()
